bodies.name: Polymele
bodies.credit: Levison et al. (2023), ACM abstract 2184; Levison et al. (2025), Space Science Reviews 221, 70
bodies.shapeMeaning: Published approximate ellipsoid from six stellar occultations, assuming the satellite's orbit is circular and equatorial.
bodies.orientationMeaning: The fitted pole assumes an equatorial satellite orbit. Rotation period and current longitude remain unqualified; the display meridian is arbitrary.
bodies.introduction: Polymele is a very flattened Jupiter Trojan and a Lucy target. This published ellipsoid is constrained by stellar occultations and its satellite's projected position. The grid marks unmapped terrain.
unresolved: The selected model does not establish a current rotational phase or an unambiguous period.
The satellite is outside this standalone asteroid package.

bodies.name: Leucus
bodies.credit: Mottola et al. (2020), The Planetary Science Journal 1, 73; Levison et al. (2025), Space Science Reviews 221, 70
bodies.shapeMeaning: Ellipsoid approximation using the published convex model's maximum dimensions, as summarized by the Lucy mission paper. It does not reproduce the original irregular convex mesh or occultation silhouettes.
bodies.orientationMeaning: Published prograde pole, with an arbitrary display meridian. The approximation has no qualified current surface longitude.
bodies.introduction: Leucus is an elongated Jupiter Trojan with an unusually slow rotation. This ellipsoid approximates the dimensions of the published light-curve and occultation model; its irregular outline is unresolved here. The grid marks unmapped terrain.
unresolved: The original Mottola 2020 convex mesh was not located in the checked paper's supporting release.
DAMIT models 6692 and 6693 have different poles and no matched absolute scale; their geometry is not mixed with this solution.

bodies.name: Orus
bodies.credit: Mottola et al. (2023), The Planetary Science Journal 4, 18, Table 3; Levison et al. (2025), Space Science Reviews 221, 70
bodies.shapeMeaning: Ellipsoid approximation using the published convex model's maximum dimensions, as summarized by the Lucy mission paper. The original convex mesh and local concavities are not represented.
bodies.orientationMeaning: Published retrograde pole, with an arbitrary display meridian. The approximation has no qualified current surface longitude.
bodies.introduction: Orus is a dark Jupiter Trojan selected for Lucy's exploration of the leading swarm. This ellipsoid approximates the dimensions of the published light-curve and occultation model. The grid marks unmapped terrain.
unresolved: The checked paper's supporting material contains observation tables; an original downloadable convex mesh was not located.
The paper's 60.5 km surface-equivalent diameter is not a volume-equivalent diameter and is not used to rescale this approximation.

bodies.name: Eurybates
bodies.credit: Mottola et al. (2023), The Planetary Science Journal 4, 18, Table 3
bodies.shapeMeaning: Authored ellipsoid approximation constrained to the published convex model's maximum extents. These are not independently measured ellipsoid axes; the irregular convex outline and model volume are not reproduced.
bodies.orientationMeaning: Published retrograde pole, with an arbitrary display meridian. The approximation has no qualified current surface longitude.
bodies.introduction: Eurybates is a Jupiter Trojan and the largest remnant of a collisional family. This approximate ellipsoid preserves the published model's overall extents, while its irregular outline remains unresolved. The grid marks unmapped terrain.
unresolved: The original 1454-facet convex reconstruction was not located in the checked paper's supporting release.
The paper's 69.3 km surface-equivalent diameter is not a volume-equivalent diameter and is not used to rescale this approximation.
Queta is outside this standalone asteroid package.

bodies.name: Patroclus
bodies.credit: Buie et al. (2015), The Astronomical Journal 149, 113; existing JPL#82 Patroclus-Menoetius source closure
bodies.shapeMeaning: Published primary-component ellipsoid combining occultation and light-curve constraints. Its full axes differ from the two-dimensional occultation limb and from the unresolved binary system's radiometric diameter.
bodies.orientationMeaning: Synchronous spin-axis approximation using the same 2024 orbital pole as Menoetius; arbitrary display meridian. A physical mutual-event phase is not claimed.
bodies.introduction: Patroclus and Menoetius form a large Trojan binary that Lucy will visit in the trailing swarm. This published ellipsoid represents Patroclus alone. The grid marks unmapped terrain.
unresolved: Local shape deviations and a physical mutual-event rotational phase remain unqualified.
The existing Menoetius package supplies the retained primary-specific heliocentric state; the system barycentre is not substituted for Patroclus.
